scan.summary: This is your written Emergency Action Plan for the Portland facility. It covers alarm signals, evacuation and shelter-in-place, headcounts, first aid and training. In Oregon the rule that governs it is Oregon OSHA's own emergency action plan rule, OAR 437-002-0042, which replaces the federal 29 CFR 1910.38. The plan is well built on evacuation, headcounts and alarm signals. It is missing some required parts: how to report an emergency, how to shut down equipment before leaving, and who to contact. It has also not been revised since February 2021, even though it says it is reviewed every January.
scan.freshness_note: The last revision is February 2021, about five years and seven months ago. Section 6 says the facilities lead reviews the plan every January, but nothing in the file shows a review in 2022 through 2026. Ask the facilities lead for any review records. If there are none, review the plan, re-date it and re-issue it.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan says pull stations are at each exit and that the alarm is monitored. It never tells employees how to report an emergency: who calls 911, what to say, or how to report a chemical release or medical emergency that the fire alarm does not cover.
gaps.fix: Add a short reporting procedure. For example: pull the nearest station for a fire, call 911 from any phone, then tell the facilities lead or incident coordinator, and give the emergency phone numbers.
gaps.locator: not in the document (would belong in Section 2 or 3)
gaps.quote: Manual pull stations are located at each exit door.

gaps.title: No procedure for shutting down critical equipment before evacuating
gaps.description: The only shutdown described is the ventilation shutdown during shelter-in-place. The plan does not say whether anyone stays behind to shut down laboratory equipment, chemical transfer or filling operations, forklifts or dock equipment before leaving. If no one stays behind, the plan should say so plainly.
gaps.fix: Add a section on critical operations. Name each piece of equipment, the job title responsible for shutting it down and the point at which that person must leave. Or state that no employee remains to operate equipment and that everyone leaves immediately.
gaps.quote: all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit

gaps.title: No names or job titles of people to contact about the plan
gaps.description: The plan does not list anyone employees can contact for more information about the plan or their duties under it. The federal rule requires this, and I believe the Oregon rule does too. I confirmed Oregon's parts (a) through (d) but did not see the full text of the later parts.
gaps.fix: Add a contacts section with the name or job title and phone number of the plan owner (for example, the facilities lead) and of the incident coordinator.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2); the same element is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(6) in the federal rule. I did not confirm the exact Oregon subsection number.

gaps.title: Incident coordinator role never assigned
gaps.description: Section 4 relies on an incident coordinator to receive the headcount and give the all-clear, but the plan never says which person or job title fills that role. The roster is described as listing wardens and first-aid responders only.
gaps.fix: Name the job title that serves as incident coordinator, plus a backup for each shift. Add them to the Appendix B roster.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(b), procedures to account for all employees. This is my reading of the rule.
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point

gaps.title: No instructions for a chemical spill or release inside the building
gaps.description: For a chemical distributor this is the most likely emergency. The plan covers outdoor releases (shelter in place) and exposed employees (eyewash). It does not say what employees do about a spill or release inside the warehouse or lab: whether they evacuate and call outside responders, or whether trained staff respond. If any employees respond to releases beyond small incidental spills, the federal emergency response rule (HAZWOPER, 29 CFR 1910.120(q)) applies, and I believe Oregon adopts it. That rule requires a separate emergency response plan and training.
gaps.fix: Say which approach the company takes. Either all employees evacuate and outside responders are called, which relies on this plan, or name the trained spill responders and point to a separate spill or emergency response plan.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q)(1) and (q)(2). I believe Oregon adopts this by reference in Division 2, Subdivision H, but did not check the Oregon adoption.
gaps.locator: Section 3 (would belong in Section 3 or a new section)
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds.

gaps.title: Silent on who may use fire extinguishers
gaps.description: The plan does not say whether employees fight small fires or all evacuate. Oregon's portable fire extinguisher rule relaxes some training requirements when an emergency action plan says which employees may use extinguishers and requires everyone else to evacuate.
gaps.fix: State who, if anyone, is trained and allowed to use extinguishers, and that all other employees evacuate.
gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0187 (portable fire extinguishers). I did not confirm the exact subsection.

gaps.title: No record that the promised January reviews happened
gaps.description: The plan commits to a review every January, yet the revision date is still February 2021 and there is no review log or sign-off. The rule may not require this review, but it is the company's own written commitment, and an inspector may ask for evidence of it.
gaps.fix: Add a review log (date, reviewer, changes made) to the plan. Complete and record a review now, including any changes in headcount, layout or staff roles since 2021.
gaps.citation: The plan's own commitment in Section 6. No specific rule citation.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

gaps.title: Appendices A and B not in the file
gaps.description: The evacuation maps (Appendix A) and the warden and first-aid roster (Appendix B) are listed but not attached. Exit route assignments and the people assigned to duties cannot be checked without them.
gaps.fix: Attach the current maps and roster to the file copy, and check that the roster names current employees.
gaps.quote: Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
